newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FOCUS - Sceptical Taiwan says rival China must bend.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Sceptical Taiwan says rival China must bend.

text.p: With Hong Kong safely back in the nest, Beijing is turning its attentions to a far wilier quarry -- the Chinese Nationalist-ruled island fortress of Taiwan.

Though just 200 km (125 miles) off China's southeast shore, Taiwan has eluded capture for five decades, resisting Chairman Mao Zedong's bombast and bombs and successor Deng Xiaoping's promise of lucrative chunks of the mainland's "socialist market economy".
Now, communist China's third leader, Jiang Zemin, has staked his legacy to Taiwan with an eight-point plan for its "peaceful reunification with the motherland" launched in 1995.
At the plan's heart is Deng's brainchild: a "one country, two systems" pledge of political, economic and even military autonomy, as long as Taiwan accepts Beijing's sovereignty.

On his triumphal return to Beijing on Monday after taking the reins of Hong Kong, Jiang palpably turned up the heat on the exiled Republic of China government that fled to Taiwan in 1949 after losing the mainland to the communists in a civil war.
"The prospect of complete national reunification... now stands promisingly in sight," Jiang said, calling Hong Kong's return a major victory toward China's peaceful reunification.
Premier Li Peng put Beijing's ambitions more directly.
"The 'one country, two systems' formula works for Hong Kong and Macau," Li said. "It can also work for Taiwan."
With Hong Kong now giving "one country, two systems" a whirl, can Jiang and Li succeed where Mao and Deng failed?
Taiwan, deeply sceptical and defensive, rejects the concept outright, saying Taiwanese were unlikely to jeopardise one of Asia's liveliest democracies to accept communist sovereignty.
"We must respect the wishes of the people," Premier Lien Chan said after Hong Kong's handover. "We cannot use their welfare as a bargaining chip in negotiating or dealmaking."
"I don't think anyone on this island will voluntarily accept communism as a system of society or a system of government."
Taiwan is determined to turn the critical focus back onto the mainland, arguing that all cross-straits differences arise from the iron-fisted absolutism of China's Communist Party.
Lien said Beijing had been forced to dream up "one country, two systems" because imposing Chinese communism would have killed off Hong Kong's freedoms and prosperity.
Taiwan, he said, could never countenance reunification under anything short of multiparty democracy across all of China -- a scheme he dubbed "one country, one good system".

Despite Jiang Zemin's new appeals, Beijing has made clear it is in no hurry to regain Taiwan and that this was a project for the next century -- as long as Taipei sticks to the status quo and does not attempt a formal break.
Mindful of Beijing's unbending threat to retake Taiwan by force if necessary, the Republic of China has clung tenaciously to its sovereignty, with one of Asia's top armies at the ready.

As a target for absorption, British-ruled Hong Kong was puny by comparison with Taiwan, a fortress-like sovereign state once nicknamed an "unsinkable aircraft carrier" when it was the front line in the West's Cold War containment of communism in Asia.

Today, though pinched tighter by China's diplomatic embargo, Taiwan still manages to arm itself. It is no coincidence that major shipments of western warplanes, warships and missiles began arriving in the runup to Hong Kong's handover.
Still, it is probably Taiwan's fast-developing democracy, not its military prowess, that most complicates China's ambitions to recover the island.

Experts say Beijing, already wary of the free expression it has pledged to tolerate in Hong Kong, is more deeply troubled by moves to add the power of referendum to Taiwan's constitution -- giving people a tool of self-determination.
For now, Taiwan public opinion splits with neat symmetry.

Big centrist pluralities of 30-40 percent favour eventual union or eventual independence but still support the status quo for now. At the extremes, minorities of about eight percent favour immediate moves toward independence or China union.
It's a balance that Beijing hopes to tip -- towards reunion -- through effective implementation of "one country, two systems" in Hong Kong.
Taiwan and its 21 million people will be watching.
